en-36: x series firmware upgrade file controller(mainboard) firmware upgrade file old: [download mainboard firmware 1.0] new: [download mainboard firmware 2.0] hmi(panel) upgrade file old: [download control panel firmware 1.0] new: [download control panel firmware 2.0] how to select the correct firmware upgrade file firmware upgrade guide (for x series users) x series firmware upgrade video tutorial 1. updating control board firmware 1.1 updating control board firmware via rdwords (only for windows users) 1.install the rdworks program on your computer. 2.connect the device to the computer using a data cable and start rdworks. 3.click "system setting" - "controller" to enter the controller upgrade interface.enter "rd8888" in the "vendor password" input field and click the "input" button to confirm the password. 4.click "upgrade firmware". in the pop-up window, find and select the corresponding motherboard firmware upgrade file, wait and confirm that the upgrade is complete. 5.click "ok" to close the prompt window. restart the device. caution: be sure to select an upgrade file that matches the controller. (you can check the bar code label on the motherboard to determine whether it is new or old. the old motherboard number has "1g" and the new motherboard does not.) cannot upgrade compared to the lower upgrade file of the current controller. restart the device after the upgrade. 1.2 updating control board firmware via makerboost (panel firmware upgrade support will be added in a future update) 1.launch makerboost and click "switch" to connect to the xrf/xt machine. 2.open "settings", select "vendor setting", and enter the password: tl9501. 3.after clicking "system", select "firmware upgrade". upload the corresponding device firmware file. wait for the upgrade process to complete. power off the device completely, then restart it to finalize the controller firmware upgrade. caution: must select a firmware file exactly matching your controller model.(the selection method is the same as mentioned above) never attempt to downgrade (e.g. installing firmware older than the current version). during the controller firmware upgrade process, do not power off the device, disconnect the computer from the device, or press any buttons on the equipment. 2. updating panel firmware via tf card 1.use a blank tf card, a card reader, and a docking station to connect the tf card to your computer. 2.open “disk utility” and format the tf card to ensure the file system is fat32. 3.extract the front panel firmware upgrade files to the root directory of the tf card. then safely eject the tf card from your mac and remove it. 4.ensure the device is powered off completely. remove the right-side protective cover of the control panel, then insert the tf card into the tf card slot at the bottom of the control panel. 5. power on the device. the front panel will automatically begin updating. when the screen displays “sd card process...end!”, the upgrade is complete. power off the device, remove the tf card, and then power it on again to finalize the upgrade.
en-263: air assist is essential for blowing away soot and suppressing flare-ups during laser processing. however, if your air pump continues to run indefinitely long after your project has finished, it causes unnecessary noise, wear, and power consumption. this guide explains why your air assist pump fails to shut off automatically and provides a quick fix along with a breakdown of your machine's air assist operating logic. problem description the layer settings are configured to keep air assist on during cutting layers in lightburn. the laser turns on air assist correctly when cutting begins. however, after the entire processing job finishes, the air assist remains running continuously and fails to shut off even after 10–15 minutes. cause the air pump is currently plugged into an external outlet rather than the machine's dedicated power port. while the machine's internal solenoid valve can toggle airflow routing, it cannot cut power to an independently powered external pump. consequently, the air pump continues running indefinitely after the job completes. solution plug the air pump's power cable directly into the dedicated air pump power socket located on the rear panel of the machine. this routing allows the mainboard's internal relay to automatically control power state switching alongside job execution. then run a test job to verify normal shutoff functionality. air assist operating logic: 1. airflow intensity by layer type: airflow strength is governed automatically by the active layer operation rather than the toggle switch in lightburn. engraving layers trigger low airflow, whereas cutting layers trigger high airflow. toggling the "air assist" switch on/off within lightburn layer properties will not override this native behavior. 2. post-job smoke purge delay: after a job finishes, the equipment is programmed to keep the air pump running for approximately 20 seconds before switching off to purge any residual smoke and fumes from the work area. important reminder: if these steps do not resolve the issue, please submit a support ticket on zoho: https://zohodesk.1laser.com/portal/en/newticket . a technician will then be able to conduct a more in-depth diagnosis and resolve your problem.
en-72: this air assist system features start-stop interlock control with the laser equipment: the air assist system automatically activates / deactivates when the laser equipment is started / shut down. if the laser equipment has no active processing task, the air assist system stops air supply. 4.2 digital pressure gauge 4.2.1 panel overview 4.2.2 function & usage the digital pressure gauge within this air assist kit has undergone precision calibration prior to shipment. users must not disassemble or recalibrate the gauge. the gauge provides real-time, continuous display of the pressure value detected by the sensor. when system pressure is stable with minimal fluctuation, the gauge reading will remain clear and steady. important: if you observe that the digital pressure gauge only displays up to 0.5 mpa when using a 0.6 mpa air supply, this is a normal occurrence. pressure reduction occurs as the air enters the system, and this level of drop falls within the expected range. 4.2.3 output display & error codes during normal operation, the gauge continuously displays the real-time air pressure value. upon detecting a system abnormality, the screen will display one of the following error codes: error display error description abnormal current consumption on switch output pressure applied during zero-point calibration pressure value exceeds measurement range internal error internal error if an error code appears: do not force continued operation. this may damage the laser equipment and air assist kit. please contact after-sales support personnel for resolution. 4.2.4 safety precautions gas compatibility: use only with non-corrosive gases. strictly prohibited for use with corrosive gases, flammable gases, or any liquids. physical handling: the gauge must not be subjected to dropping, impact, or severe shock. such events may cause permanent damage to internal precision components, resulting in gauge failure. input pressure limits: input pressure must remain strictly within the specified pressure and rated voltage limits. exceeding the upper limit will cause damage to the pressure gauge and related internal components. operating environment: do not use the gauge in environments with excessive moisture, oil mist, dust, or other contaminants. contaminant ingress can lead to internal air path blockage, corrosion of precision parts, or functional failure. 4.3 controlling air assist pressure modes the air assist control supports controlling the auxiliary air pressure in two modes: high pressure and low pressure. the air pressure settings for each mode are independent. you can control the air assist control's operating mode via the following methods: automatic control via device processing: when the device is processing a design, it automatically controls the air assist control's operating mode based on the air assist settings defined in the design layers. manual control: when the device is not in processing mode and manual control mode is inactive (both button leds are off), press the high-pressure air test button or the low-pressure air test button to manually control the air assist control's operating mode. 4.3.1 setting air assist control mode in design software after correct installation, the device will automatically set the air assist control's pressure mode based on the air assist switch settings defined in the design layers: using makerboost: double-click the design layer. in the pop-up window, set air assist to low or high. selecting high sets the layer for high-pressure air assist. selecting low sets the layer for low-pressure air assist. using rdworks: double-click the design layer. in the pop-up window, set if blowing to yes to enable high-pressure air assist for that layer. setting it to no enables low-pressure air assist. using lightburn: double-click the design layer. in the pop-up window, set air assist to on to enable high-pressure air assist for that layer. setting it to off enables low-pressure air assist. 4.3.2 adjusting high-pressure air assist ensure only the high-pressure air test button led is illuminated. if the led is off, press the button or ensure the device is processing with the current layer set to air assist on (high). pull up the high-pressure air adjustment knob to disengage its lock. rotate clockwise to increase high-pressure air assist. rotate counterclockwise to decrease high-pressure air assist. observe the value on the digital display until the desired pressure is reached. push down the knob to re-engage its lock. 4.3.3 adjusting low-pressure air assist ensure only the low-pressure air test button led is illuminated. if the led is off, press the button or ensure the device is processing with the current layer set to air assist on (low). pull up the low-pressure air adjustment knob to disengage its lock. rotate clockwise to increase low-pressure air assist. rotate counterclockwise to decrease low-pressure air assist. observe the value on the digital display until the desired pressure is reached. push down the knob to re-engage its lock. 4.3.4 low-pressure operation protection typically, higher air pressure is used for cutting operations, while lower pressure yields better results for engraving operations. you can adjust the air pressure to meet specific requirements via manual knob adjustment or by changing the air assist mode in your design. critical protection mechanism: when air assist pressure is too low (supply pressure < 0.3 psi / ~2.07 kpa) or air supply is interrupted, the airflow from the laser nozzle may be insufficient to protect the lens and nozzle from smoke and debris contamination. under these conditions, the air assist control will automatically halt operation and may display a warning message on the screen. re-adjust the corresponding pressure adjustment knob until the pressure display returns to a green (normal) indication, then resume processing. 4.4 troubleshooting if the following issues occur during use, contact after-sales service: symptom pos
en-226: this guide explains why the air assist pressure may remain static despite adjusting the knob and pressing the "test" button, and provides step-by-step troubleshooting methods to restore proper pressure control. problem description when pressing the "test" button, the inlet pressure value displayed on the digital gauge remains identical to the idle value (before pressing the button). turning the adjustment knob does not change the live reading, and the value stays locked at the initial pressure. source: image provided by a customer only after releasing the button does the pressure reading slowly drift toward the newly adjusted setting, taking 3 to 5 minutes to finally stabilize. cause air source issues: an incorrect setting or limitation on the air supply itself (air pump or air compressor). pneumatic leak: a leak or loose connection anywhere along the air lines. gauge lockout: the digital gauge is stuck in lock mode, which can cause reading and refresh anomalies. restricted valve: an internal air pipe valve is overtightened, choking off the airflow entirely. hardware fault: internal component damage inside the air assist kit itself. solution method 1. inspect the air source and tubing check the built-in air pump (for x series) or your external air compressor to ensure they are powered on and delivering adequate pressure. inspect the external air lines feeding into the air assist kit. ensure all push-to-connect fittings are seated firmly and check the tubing for punctures, crimps, or leaks. method 2. unlock and reset the digital gauge (if locked) if you notice a key icon on the left side of the digital display, it is locked. press and hold both the "s" and "▼" buttons simultaneously. after a few seconds, the main screen will display "lock" and the sub-screen will read "off", indicating a successful unlock. disconnect the main air supply line. press and hold both the "▲" and "▼" buttons until the displayed reading returns to exactly 0. reconnect the air source, press the "test" button, and turn the knob to check if it now regulates properly. method 3. inspect internal air valves hydra gen1 series locate the air pipe needle valve on the back of the x-axis guide rail. check if the needle valve has been turned completely tight, choking the airflow. while maintaining safety, place a tissue beneath the laser nozzle to feel for air output while turning the needle valve. adjust it until you feel a steady stream of air and the air assist kit gauge begins to update fluidly. x series remove the laser head cover to expose the valve connected to the end of the internal air tubing. please refer to this guide for step-by-step adjustment instructions: how to adjust the air pipe screw ⚠️ important note if none of the methods above resolve the issue, it is likely that an internal component within the air assist kit is defective. please document your troubleshooting results and contact onelaser after-sales support for assistance with a replacement part. important reminder: if these steps do not resolve the issue, please click this link to submit a support ticket: https://zohodesk.1laser.com/portal/en/newticket . a technician will then be able to conduct a more in-depth diagnosis and resolve your problem.

en-276: achieving a precise focal point is critical for clean vector cuts and sharp raster engravings. when an automatic focus cycle completes but leaves the nozzle tip too close to or too far from the material, the resulting defocusing leads to poor engraving contrast, incomplete material penetration, or excessively thick burn marks. this guide walks you through verifying your sensor hardware and resetting software focus parameters to restore optimal laser performance. problem description after running an autofocus cycle, the distance between the laser nozzle tip and the material surface is either too large or too small. this defocusing causes poor engraving quality, weak cutting penetration, or excessively wide kerf marks. cause corrupted/modified parameters: software focal length parameters or homing offset values have been altered. sensor hardware fault: the autofocus physical probe or optical sensor mechanism is malfunctioning or reporting intermittent signals. solution step 1. verify autofocus sensor hardware status please refer to the autofocus troubleshooting guide and complete all recommended hardware diagnostic checks. if the sensor hardware passes inspection but the focal gap remains incorrect, proceed to step 2. step 2. inspect and reset focal parameters in software two primary settings govern the autofocus stop distance: focus distance and the z-axis home offset . in lightburn, navigate to edit > machine settings . locate and check the following two parameters against factory default values: focus distance: factory backup baseline is typically 1.900 mm . z-axis home offset: factory baseline is typically set to 4.000 mm . manually input the default values into the respective fields and click write to upload the config to the controller. or you can contact onelaser after-sales support to request the machine's original factory backup file. import the backup file into lightburn and write it to the machine. finally, restart the equipment, perform an autofocus cycle, and measure the nozzle-to-material clearance to confirm normal focal distance is restored. important reminder: if these steps do not resolve the issue, please submit a support ticket on zoho: https://zohodesk.1laser.com/portal/en/newticket . a technician will then be able to conduct a more in-depth diagnosis and resolve your problem.
en-274: this troubleshooting guide explains why your x series rf laser tube may temporarily lose power mid-operation and provides step-by-step methods to resolve overheating issues, restore continuous beam output, and complete your processing jobs without interruption. problem description during cutting, the laser suddenly stops emitting a beam and then randomly resumes firing later, leaving parts of the job incompletely cut. this issue frequently occurs when a job is 80% to 99% complete, though the exact timestamp varies every time. example: a recent job running at 5 mm/s speed and 100% power (100% continuous output for roughly 30 minutes) experienced this mid-process beam drop. cause unsuitable ambient environment: the surrounding room temperature exceeds the operating threshold for the air-cooled rf laser tube. thermal overload / overheating: prolonged operation at maximum power generates excess thermal energy faster than the cooling fans can dissipate it. the rf tube enters a temporary thermal protection shutdown mode until internal temperatures cool down. solution method 1. verify and regulate ambient temperature check the temperature of your workspace. rf laser tubes require an ambient operating temperature strictly between 0℃ and 35℃ (32℉ to 95℉). users operating in garages, unconditioned sheds, or hot summer environments easily exceed these safe limits. if the machine cannot be moved to a temperature-controlled environment, avoid running long-duration jobs at 100% full power. manufacturer environmental specifications: operating temperature 0-35℃ (32-95℉) operating humidity ≤95% (air-cooled, non-condensing) operating altitude ≤2000m * data retrieved from the official rf tube manufacturer manual. method 2. maximize cooling fan power step 1. inspect diagnostic led indicators when the laser beam cuts out mid-job, open the rear access panel of the machine to locate the fan control board. check whether the d1, d2, or d5 diagnostic leds are illuminated. step 2. adjust fan speed mode an illuminated d2 led indicates that the rf tube has reached an over-temperature state. locate the fan speed toggle switch on the fan control board and slide it all the way to the far right position to force the cooling fans to operate continuously at max power. re-run the processing job to verify if increased airflow resolves the thermal throttling and restores continuous laser output. important reminder: if these steps do not resolve the issue, please submit a support ticket on zoho: https://zohodesk.1laser.com/portal/en/newticket . a technician will then be able to conduct a more in-depth diagnosis and resolve your problem.

en-261: overview leather is a flexible and heat-sensitive material that requires careful control during laser cutting. while laser processing can create precise shapes and clean edges, improper settings, unsuitable materials, or insufficient machine preparation may result in problems such as excessive burning, incomplete cutting, deformation, and inconsistent results. because leather varies significantly depending on animal source, tanning method, thickness, dye, and surface coating, the same laser parameters may not work for every material. this guide explains common leather laser cutting problems, their possible causes, and recommended solutions. problem 1: leather does not cut through completely possible causes laser power is too low. cutting speed is too high. focus position is incorrect. leather thickness varies. the lens or mirrors are contaminated. the material density is higher than expected. the leather contains coatings that reduce laser penetration. recommended solutions increase laser power gradually. reduce cutting speed. verify the focus distance. clean optical components. perform test cuts on the actual leather batch. check whether the material composition is suitable for laser processing. for thick leather, multiple passes may produce better results than excessive power in a single pass. problem 2: leather edges are too dark or burned possible causes laser power is too high. cutting speed is too slow. excessive heat accumulation. air assist is insufficient. exhaust airflow is inadequate. the material contains oils or coatings that increase burning. recommended solutions reduce laser power. increase cutting speed. improve air assist airflow. verify exhaust performance. clean the lens and mirrors. test different settings on scrap material. a slightly darkened edge is normal for leather because organic fibers carbonize during laser processing. excessive burning usually indicates excessive heat input. problem 3: cut edges become hard or brittle possible causes excessive laser energy. slow cutting speed. multiple passes creating too much heat. leather contains a high amount of oil or coating. recommended solutions reduce power and increase speed. avoid unnecessary repeated passes. optimize cutting parameters for the specific leather type. use lower energy settings for soft leather. excessive heat can change the natural properties of leather and reduce flexibility. problem 4: leather warps, curls, or shrinks after cutting possible causes heat accumulation during cutting. material is too thin or lightweight. leather contains moisture. the material is not properly secured. airflow moves the material during processing. recommended solutions reduce laser energy. increase cutting speed. secure the leather properly. use a vacuum table or low-tack masking when appropriate. store leather in a stable environment before processing. thin leather is especially sensitive to heat and should be tested carefully. problem 5: pu leather melts or leaves sticky residue possible causes synthetic coating reacts poorly to laser heat. laser power is too high. cutting speed is too slow. the material contains unsuitable polymers. recommended solutions verify the pu leather composition. reduce laser power. increase cutting speed. improve exhaust airflow. test another material sample. some synthetic leather products are not suitable for laser processing due to their coating composition. problem 6: strong smoke or unpleasant odor during cutting possible causes leather contains dyes, oils, or tanning chemicals. synthetic coatings release additional fumes. exhaust airflow is insufficient. air assist is inadequate. recommended solutions verify the material composition. improve ventilation. increase exhaust efficiency. maintain proper air assist. avoid processing unknown synthetic leather. warning materials containing pvc or unknown chemical coatings should not be laser processed without verification. problem 7: cutting lines are uneven possible causes leather surface is not flat. material moves during processing. focus distance changes across the cutting area. the laser beam is not aligned correctly. the cutting table is uneven. recommended solutions flatten the material before cutting. use appropriate fixation methods. check focus consistency. verify machine alignment. confirm that the work surface is level. flexible materials require better preparation than rigid sheets. problem 8: small details are not cut correctly possible causes cutting speed is too high. laser spot size is too large. excessive heat affects small features. the material moves during processing. recommended solutions use a shorter focal length lens when appropriate. reduce cutting speed for detailed areas. optimize power settings. secure the material more effectively. for complex leather patterns, accurate focus and stable material positioning are especially important. problem 9: smoke stains appear around cut areas possible causes weak exhaust airflow. insufficient air assist. excessive laser power. leather surface absorbs smoke residue. recommended solutions improve exhaust performance. adjust air assist. reduce laser energy. use protective masking when suitable. clean the surface carefully after processing. light-colored leather is usually more sensitive to smoke staining. problem 10: different areas of the same leather sheet cut differently possible causes natural variation in leather structure. uneven thickness. different moisture levels. different surface treatments. recommended solutions measure material thickness before production. perform test cuts in different areas. sort leather pieces by similar characteristics. adjust production methods for natural material variation. unlike manufactured sheets, genuine leather naturally contains variations. problem 11: the cutting quality suddenly becomes worse possible causes dirty lens or mirrors. reduced laser power output. blocked air assist nozzle. poor exhaust performance. incorrect focus afte
en-262: overview leather engraving is one of the most popular applications of laser processing because it allows users to create personalized designs, logos, patterns, text, and decorative details while preserving the natural appearance of the material. unlike laser cutting, engraving does not separate the material. instead, the laser removes or modifies the surface layer of leather to create visible contrast through changes in texture, color, and surface structure. however, leather is a natural and highly variable material. the engraving result depends on leather type, tanning method, surface coating, color, thickness, and moisture content. this guide explains best practices for laser engraving leather and provides recommendations for achieving clear, consistent, and professional engraving results. how laser engraving works on leather leather is mainly composed of collagen fibers that react to heat from the laser beam. during engraving: the laser removes or modifies the surface fibers. the treated area becomes darker due to carbonization. the surface texture changes, creating visual contrast. the engraved pattern becomes visible. the final appearance depends on: leather composition surface finish laser energy processing speed resolution settings unlike acrylic or coated metals, leather engraving is highly dependent on natural material characteristics. choosing the right leather for engraving different leather types produce different engraving effects. vegetable-tanned leather vegetable-tanned leather is one of the most recommended materials for laser engraving. advantages: strong engraving contrast natural surface clear details develops unique aging effects common applications: wallets notebook covers keychains handmade leather goods full-grain leather full-grain leather retains the natural grain structure of the hide. engraving characteristics: natural texture remains visible results vary slightly between pieces premium appearance suitable for: luxury accessories high-end customization top-grain leather top-grain leather has a more processed surface. advantages: more consistent appearance predictable engraving results smooth surface suitable for: commercial products branding applications suede and nubuck leather suede and nubuck have soft fiber surfaces. engraving considerations: lower contrast may occur. excessive heat can damage the texture. use careful power control. pu leather pu leather can create attractive engraving effects when the surface coating is suitable. possible effects: removing colored en-264: if your autofocus assembly has been physically damaged and you are relying on manual focusing while waiting for replacement parts, you may find that the z-axis bed refuses to move upward. this guide explains why your laser's safety logic locks out upward movement and provides a step-by-step wiring bypass to temporarily restore manual z-axis control. problem description the autofocus assembly is damaged. while waiting for replacement parts, manual focusing must be used. however, when adjusting the z-axis height using the control panel, the bed can only move downward and refuses to move upward. cause under the motherboard's built-in safety logic, a damaged or disconnected autofocus sensor continuously reports a "triggered" status. because the controller assumes the autofocus sensor is actively tripped (indicating the material is already touching the focus head), it locks out all upward z-axis movement to prevent a collision with the laser head. solution to manually restore upward z-axis movement: locate the two wires running from the motherboard to the autofocus sensor ---- the yellow-green wire and the black wire. short-circuit these two wires together. this signals a closed state to the motherboard, bypassing the lock and restoring upward control. ⚠️ safety warning overriding the z-axis safety limitation removes collision protection. exercise extreme caution when moving the platform upward manually to prevent the bed or material from crashing into the laser head, which can cause component damage or even bend the x-axis guide rail. important reminder: if these steps do not resolve the issue, please submit a support ticket on zoho: https://zohodesk.1laser.com/portal/en/newticket . a technician will then be able to conduct a more in-depth diagnosis and resolve your problem.

en-257: automatic focusing simplifies job setup, but if your laser head stops descending midway before touching the material, your focal distance will be completely off. this troubleshooting guide addresses why your z-axis stops lowering prematurely—often while displaying z: 0.000 on the control panel—and provides clear steps to resolve software parameter caps, sensor jams, and cable strain. problem description the laser head stops moving downward midway before reaching the bottom limit of the lead screw, preventing autofocus from reaching its minimum height. at the same time, the control panel displays the z-axis coordinate as already having reached 0.000. source: image provided by a customer cause incorrect software limits: the max travel value for the z-axis in machine settings was modified. stuck autofocus sensor trigger: the physical trigger pin inside the autofocus sensor is jammed, causing the sensor to continuously report a triggered state so the system controller assumes the head has hit its limit. restricted cables or air tubing: over time, the autofocus wiring harness or air assist tube has slipped out from the back of the laser head assembly. as the head travels downward, it pulls the lines taut, mechanically stopping further downward travel. solution step 1. check software parameters open machine settings in lightburn and expand the z axis settings menu. verify that the max travel parameter is correctly set to 50. if it differs, update the value to 50, write the settings to the controller, and test again. source: image provided by a customer step 2. inspect the autofocus sensor use your finger to gently push the central trigger block of the autofocus sensor upward and release it. verify whether it springs back smoothly or remains jammed in the middle of the sensor housing. step 3. inspect cable and air tube clearance inspect the rear of the laser head for any pulled-tight wiring or air tubing. gently pull a small amount of slack back into the laser head enclosure until there is sufficient strain relief and the head can move down through its full range of motion without pulling on the lines. source: image provided by a customer important reminder: if these steps do not resolve the issue, please submit a support ticket on zoho: https://zohodesk.1laser.com/portal/en/newticket . a technician will then be able to conduct a more in-depth diagnosis and resolve your problem.
en-256: on dual-source hydra series machines, switching between rotary attachment usage and standard rf tube processing relies on an automated motorized mirror elevation mechanism. if the first mirror (m1) mount remains stuck in the lowered position after disconnecting your rotary, the rf laser beam will be blocked from entering the optical path. this guide provides step-by-step instructions to restore proper mirror elevation through correct software sequencing, hardware checks, and driver verification. problem description after using the rotary and processing with the rf tube again, no laser exits the laser head nozzle. upon inspecting the first mirror assembly, the mirror mount is found stuck in the lowered position, causing the rf laser to hit and reflect directly off the machine's metal backplate. source: image provided by a customer cause the rotary mode switch was not toggled off in the required procedural sequence after rotary operation. loose wiring connections or unseated plugs between the mount elevation motor, motor driver, and autofocus board. incorrect dip switch settings on the motor driver. the mirror elevation motor is damaged, or its lead screw is bent. solution method 1. verify the rotary toggle sequence after using the rotary, you must exit rotary mode using the following exact sequence: turn the physical rotary toggle switch on the side of the machine back on. open rotary setup in lightburn and toggle the enable rotary option to off. turn the physical rotary toggle switch on the side of the machine off. test the machine to see if the m1 mirror mount now elevates and functions properly. method 2. inspect elevation assembly components step 1. inspect the mirror elevation motor and lead screw power off the equipment completely. manually rotate the motor lead screw clockwise and counterclockwise by hand. check if the mirror mount binds, or stutters at any point along its vertical travel. if binding occurs due to a bent lead screw, the motor assembly must be replaced. note: if the driver and wiring pass inspection, a non-responsive mount may also indicate a damaged motor requiring replacement. step 2. inspect the motor driver open the lower-right access door on the back of the machine to locate the motor driver. check the diagnostic led indicator on the driver (a green light indicates normal operation) and verify that the dip switches on the driver are correctly toggled to positions 7 and 8. step 3. check cable and terminal connections inspect all wiring harnesses and connectors along the circuit path—from the autofocus board, motor driver to the m1 mount motor—to ensure no plugs have vibrated loose. the autofocus board important reminder: if these steps do not resolve the issue, please submit a support ticket on zoho: https://zohodesk.1laser.com/portal/en/newticket . a technician will then be able to conduct a more in-depth diagnosis and resolve your problem.

en-251: laser cutting has become one of the most efficient methods for processing fabrics. unlike mechanical cutting tools, a co₂ laser cuts without physical contact, eliminating blade wear while producing intricate shapes, consistent dimensions, and clean edges. for many synthetic fabrics, the laser also seals the cut edge during processing, reducing or eliminating fraying. this makes laser cutting ideal for applications ranging from fashion and upholstery to industrial textiles and custom crafts. this guide explains how laser cutting works on fabric, how to prepare your machine and materials, common processing techniques, and solutions to frequently encountered cutting issues. how laser cutting works on fabric a co₂ laser emits infrared light at a wavelength of 10.6 μm , which is readily absorbed by most organic and polymer-based fabrics. when the focused laser beam reaches the material surface, the fabric fibers rapidly heat up and either: vaporize (common with natural fibers such as cotton and linen) melt and separate (common with synthetic fibers such as polyester and nylon) because the laser never physically touches the material, there is: no blade deformation no en-99: usage — step-by-step step 1 - set the parameters after connecting the conveyor to the machine's rotary axis port, turn on the rotary axis switch located next to the port. in lightburn, open the rotary setup window and configure the following settings: rotary type：select roller, and check the box to enable rotary. rotary axis：the default selection is the y-axis (some machines may use the a-axis). parameters：input the numerical values found on the aluminum card that came with the unit into the parameter fields on the right side of the pop-up window. once configured, the conveyor is ready to use. if you encounter a length limitation when processing material with the conveyor (e.g., restricted to 500 mm): open machine settings in lightburn. find max travel within the u axis settings. change this value to 10000 and click write. the conveyor needs to be turned off and disconnected, then the machine needs to be reset or restarted before the conveyor can be reconnected to truly write the max travel value to the mainboard. step 2 - processing settings 1. we recommend selecting user origin for start from and the top left corner for job origin. this setting can reduce the occurrence of errors. 2. the width of the graph cannot exceed the working area. please note that it should not exceed the max travel of the x-axis. step 3 - after using the conveyor in lightburn, open the rotary setup window and uncheck the enable rotary box. turn off the rotary axis switch on the machine and disconnect the conveyor's cable. finally, click the reset icon on the machine's control panel to restore the machine to its normal processing state. caution: if the shutdown sequence is incorrect or if you turn off the rotary axis switch directly (skipping the lightburn disable step), it may cause homing errors or abnormal y-axis movement.
en-249: if your vertigo machine's laser head moves and fans spin normally, but no laser beam hits your material during a job or manual pulse test, you are dealing with an output cut-off. this troubleshooting guide walks you through diagnosing whether the issue stems from simple software settings, optical beam alignment, control board pre-ignition locks, or a hardware failure in the power supply or rf laser tube. problem description during a processing job, the laser head moves and the fans rotate normally, but no laser beam is emitted. no marks are left on the material, and the rf tube shows zero laser output. cause layer power settings in the file are configured too low. the beam path is severely misaligned or blocked. the equipment is still in its pre-ionization warm-up cycle. damaged power supply unit, damaged optical lenses, loose/damaged wiring harnesses or connectors, faulty fan control board port, or natural aging/failure of the rf tube. solution ⚠️ important reminder after powering on, the rf tube undergoes a pre-ionization process for up to 45 seconds. once completed, the machine will emit three beeps, indicating that the rf tube is fully ready for operation. method 1. verify layer parameters check your software laser power settings to ensure the output percentage is not set too low, which can cause the machine to appear as though it is not firing. method 2. confirm operating ambient temperature the operating ambient temperature for the laser tube must be kept strictly between 32°f and 95°f (0°c to 35°c) . operating outside this temperature range may trigger safety cutoffs or operational anomalies, resulting in no laser output from the rf tube. method 3. check direct output at the rf tube aperture remove the rear panel of the vertigo. place a small piece of wood directly in front of the rf tube exit aperture. press the pulse button on the control panel to test for direct laser output at the source: laser output present: the fault is caused by beam path misalignment or optical lens damage. proceed to method 4 to calibrate the optical path. no laser output: the issue lies within the rf tube itself, the wiring, or the power supply. method 4. inspect lenses and beam alignment inspect all mirrors, the beam combiner, and the focus lens along the optical path. cracks, burns, or severe physical damage to any optic will block the laser beam from traveling to the work surface. refer to this step-by-step alignment tutorial: how to adjust the optical path in vertigo? method 5. inspect the pre-ignition status if you do not hear the three beeps 45 seconds after powering on, open the rear cover and inspect the d5, d2, and d1 led indicators on the control board: normal status: indicators d5, d2, and d1 should all be off. abnormal status: if any led remains lit, refer to the following diagnostic guide: d5 (solid on): indicates a voltage anomaly. perform power/electrical troubleshooting. d2 (solid on): indicates the rf tube temperature is too high. the laser will lock out. stop operation, wait 4–5 minutes for the rf tube to cool down, and try again. d1 (solid on): indicates the unit is still stuck in the pre-ignition phase. wait a few extra minutes. locate the gray ethernet network cable. unplug both ends (at the fan control board and the rf tube) and firmly reconnect them. if the issue persists, swap it out with a known working ethernet cable. method 6. inspect the power supply unit prepare a multimeter. locate the power supply and check whether its green led indicator is solid on: green light solid on: use multimeter probes to measure the voltage across the +v and -v terminals. it should read 48v. an abnormal reading confirms a faulty psu. green light off: measure the input voltage across terminals l4 and n4. it should read 220v (or 110v). if input voltage is normal but the green light remains off, the psu is defective. if input voltage is abnormal, check the upstream main power wiring. method 7. inspect wiring and terminal connections locate the fanctrl board. use a multimeter to measure the voltage across the l-on and gnd terminals. it should read 5v. with the machine powered off, verify that all wiring connectors on the fan control board are firmly seated. check the primary power cables (positive and negative terminals) connected to the rf tube to ensure they are securely fastened. method 8. isolate and test the rf tube to determine whether the fault stems from the rf tube itself or an incoming control signal, perform a short-circuit diagnostic test using a standard ethernet cable: 1. take a spare ethernet cable and cut off the rj45 crystal connector at one end. 2. strip the insulation from wires 1, 3, and 7 (orange-white, green-white, brown-white) and twist them firmly together (shorted). note: this modified end remains free and does not plug into the mainboard. 3. plug the intact rj45 connector on the other end directly into the network port on the rf tube. 4. power on the machine and wait 42 seconds for the pre-ignition cycle to complete. laser fires normally: the rf tube is fully functional. the issue lies within the mainboard or control signal pipeline. no laser output: the rf tube is defective and requires replacement. important reminder: if these steps do not resolve the issue, please submit a support ticket on zoho: https://zohodesk.1laser.com/portal/en/newticket . a technician will then be able to conduct a more in-depth diagnosis and resolve your problem.
en-253: overview medium-density fiberboard (mdf) is one of the most commonly used engineered wood materials for laser cutting and engraving. its smooth surface, uniform density, and consistent internal structure make it an excellent choice for signs, decorative products, architectural models, furniture components, prototypes, and painted finished goods. unlike natural wood, mdf has no visible grain direction or internal voids, allowing laser systems to produce highly consistent cutting and engraving results across the entire sheet. however, not all mdf products are manufactured the same way. material grade, density, thickness, resin formulation, and surface finish can all influence cutting quality, smoke generation, edge appearance, and machine maintenance. this guide explains the different types of mdf and provides recommendations for selecting the most suitable material for laser processing. understanding mdf medium-density fiberboard (mdf) is an engineered wood product manufactured by compressing refined wood fibers with synthetic resin and wax under high temperature and pressure. the resulting panel has a homogeneous internal structure without natural grain or veneer layers. compared with solid wood and plywood, mdf offers several advantages for laser processing: smooth, uniform surface consistent internal density no wood grain direction predictable engraving depth excellent dimensional stability suitable for intricate cutting patterns because the material is manufactured rather than naturally grown, mdf generally provides more repeatable machining results than many natural wood products. how mdf differs from plywood although mdf and plywood are both engineered wood products, their construction and laser processing characteristics are significantly different. characteristic mdf plywood internal structure uniform wood fibers multiple wood veneer layers grain direction none visible grain in each veneer density highly consistent varies between layers surface finish smooth natural wood texture engraving appearance uniform influenced by wood grain internal voids rare possible in lower-grade plywood dust generation higher lower because mdf has a homogeneous structure, it is often preferred for projects that require smooth painted surfaces or highly consistent engraving results. understanding mdf grades different mdf grades are designed for different environments and applications. choosing the appropriate grade improves machining quality and helps avoid unnecessary processing issues. standard mdf standard mdf is the most commonly used material for laser cutting and engraving. characteristics include: uniform density smooth surface consistent engraving quality reliable cutting performance cost-effective widely available typical applications: decorative signs crafts architectural models display products boxes furniture components for most laser applications, standard mdf is the recommended choice. moisture-resistant mdf (mr mdf) moisture-resistant mdf is manufactured with modified resin systems that improve stability in humid environments. many manufacturers identify mr mdf by its green-colored core, although color may vary. typical applications include: kitchens bathrooms indoor humid environments cabinetry compared with standard mdf, mr mdf may: require slightly higher laser energy produce more smoke leave additional residue on optical components a test cut is recommended before production. fire-retardant mdf (fr mdf) fire-retardant mdf contains flame-retardant additives that improve fire resistance in commercial and architectural applications. common uses include: public buildings commercial interiors fire-rated construction although fr mdf can technically be processed by some laser systems, it is generally not recommended because flame-retardant additives may: reduce cutting efficiency produce heavier smoke leave additional residue increase optical contamination affect edge quality warning flame-retardant additives vary by manufacturer. always review the material safety documentation before attempting laser processing. high-density fiberboard (hdf) high-density fiberboard (hdf) is manufactured using finer wood fibers compressed at higher pressure than standard mdf. advantages include: higher mechanical strength better wear resistance improved dimensional stability smoother machined edges because of its higher density, hdf generally requires: higher laser power slower cutting speeds better smoke extraction more effective air assist hdf is well suited for products requiring increased durability. ultralight mdf ultralight mdf is manufactured using lower-density fibers to reduce overall weight. advantages include: easier cutting faster processing reduced machine load lightweight finished products however, it may also have: lower mechanical strength softer edges reduced screw-holding capability ultralight mdf is commonly used for decorative products and display applications. quick comparison grade laser processing suitability typical applications standard mdf ★★★★★ recommended general cutting and engraving mr mdf ★★★★☆ recommended humid indoor environments fr mdf ★☆☆☆☆ generally not recommended fire-rated construction hdf ★★★★☆ recommended durable structural components ultralight mdf ★★★★☆ recommended lightweight decorative products choosing mdf density besides grade, density also influences laser processing performance. lower-density mdf lower-density boards generally: cut more easily require less laser energy produce less heat accumulation however, they may have reduced mechanical strength and edge durability. higher-density mdf higher-density boards provide: better edge definition increased structural strength improved surface durability at the same time, they require: higher laser power slower cutting speeds improved exhaust ventilation when processing hdf or dense mdf, parameter optimization becomes more important. choosing the right thickness material thickness should match both the application
en-254: overview medium-density fiberboard (mdf) is one of the most consistent engineered wood materials for laser cutting and engraving. its homogeneous fiber structure allows for predictable machining performance, making it a popular choice for signs, decorative products, architectural models, furniture components, and painted assemblies. unlike plywood, mdf contains no veneer layers or grain direction. however, its high fiber density and resin content produce more smoke, fine dust, and residue during processing. without proper machine setup and maintenance, these by-products can reduce cutting quality and contaminate optical components. this guide provides recommended practices for laser cutting and engraving mdf, helping users achieve cleaner edges, more consistent engraving, and longer machine service life. how laser cutting works on mdf mdf is manufactured from fine wood fibers bonded with synthetic resin. during laser processing, both the wood fibers and the resin absorb laser energy. as the laser moves across the material: the wood fibers rapidly heat and vaporize. the binding resin softens, decomposes, and burns. smoke, dust, and vaporized particles are expelled from the kerf by air assist. the remaining fibers form the finished cut edge. because mdf contains significantly finer fibers than plywood, it generally produces more airborne particles and residue during cutting. maintaining effective smoke extraction is therefore essential for consistent results. selecting the appropriate lens choosing the correct focal length helps balance cutting quality, engraving detail, and material thickness. general recommendations include: lens recommended applications 1.5" fine engraving and detailed artwork 2.0" general engraving and cutting up to medium thickness 2.5" general-purpose cutting of thicker mdf 4.0" thick mdf requiring greater depth of focus short focal length lenses provide finer detail but shallower depth of focus, while longer focal length lenses improve cutting performance on thicker materials. achieving proper focus correct focus improves cutting efficiency and minimizes edge burning. a properly focused beam produces: narrow kerf width cleaner cut edges more consistent engraving depth reduced heat accumulation if the laser is focused too high: bottom edges may not cut completely. kerf width increases. cutting efficiency decreases. if the focus is too low: excessive heat accumulates near the bottom of the material. bottom edge burning increases. resin residue may build up more rapidly. for most mdf applications, focusing at or slightly below the material surface provides reliable cutting performance. tip always refocus after changing material thickness or replacing the focusing lens. optimizing power and cutting speed power and cutting speed should be adjusted together rather than independently. general recommendations include: use the minimum power required to achieve complete penetration. increase cutting speed whenever edge quality allows. avoid excessive power that produces unnecessary burning. perform parameter tests when changing mdf suppliers or thicknesses. since mdf formulations differ among manufacturers, there is no universal parameter set suitable for every board. using air assist effectively air assist plays an important role in mdf processing. proper airflow helps: remove smoke and dust from the kerf. reduce edge charring. suppress flare-ups. protect the focusing lens from contamination. improve cutting consistency. because mdf produces a large amount of fine particulate matter, insufficient air assist often results in excessive residue around the cutting area. verify that the nozzle remains clean and unobstructed throughout production. managing smoke and dust compared with plywood, mdf typically generates: more fine dust more smoke more resin vapor more optical contamination to reduce contamination: keep the exhaust system operating throughout processing. clean the honeycomb or blade table regularly. remove accumulated debris after each production run. inspect filters according to the manufacturer's maintenance schedule. effective dust management improves both machine performance and workplace cleanliness. reducing edge charring dark cut edges are a natural result of laser processing wood-based materials, but excessive charring can often be minimized. to improve edge quality: maintain accurate focus. use appropriate air assist. avoid unnecessarily slow cutting speeds. use clean optics. choose high-quality mdf with consistent density. optimize exhaust airflow. reducing heat accumulation is generally more effective than simply increasing laser power. optimizing engraving quality mdf is widely used for engraved products because its uniform structure produces consistent engraving depth. for best engraving results: use lower power than cutting operations. increase engraving speed where practical. remove surface dust before engraving. test engraving depth on scrap material. use high-resolution settings only when required. because mdf contains no visible wood grain, engraved graphics often appear more uniform than on plywood. preventing resin build-up on optics the synthetic resin used in mdf can produce sticky deposits that accumulate on optical components over time. excessive contamination may result in: reduced laser power poor cutting performance increased edge burning inconsistent engraving premature lens damage inspect and clean the lens, mirrors, and nozzle regularly using the procedures recommended by the machine manufacturer. routine maintenance is particularly important during extended mdf production runs. performing test cuts even mdf boards with similar specifications may vary in density and resin content. before beginning production: cut several small test shapes. verify complete penetration. inspect edge quality. evaluate engraving appearance if required. save successful parameter settings for future use. systematic testing helps reduce waste

en-239: the x-series laser gantry relies on precision v-wheel rubber rollers to glide smoothly across the guide rail. over time, friction, debris, or tension issues can cause these guide wheels to wear down, lose contact, or slip out of their tracks entirely. this guide will help you identify the signs of guide wheel failure and walk you through the complete adjustment or replacement process to restore perfect motion control. problem description when the laser head moves left and right, a rhythmic clicking sound is heard in sync with the rotation of the wheels. with the machine powered off, manually pushing the laser head reveals a distinct bump or catch at regular intervals. a sharp, high-pitched screeching noise occurs during x-axis movement, or the laser head jams completely on the guide rail and cannot be moved. engraved graphics show jagged edges, stair-stepping, or drift away from the intended processing path. the laser head visibly shakes or wobbles when executing high-speed directional reversals during engraving. cause the rubber guide wheels have worn down over time or developed flat spots from prolonged use. the wheels have lost contact with the guide rail, spinning freely without applying the necessary pressure. the wheels have slipped entirely out of the guide rail grooves, causing the laser head to lose its alignment constraints. solution whether you need to replace worn wheels (if your machine is under warranty, please contact onelaser after-sales support to receive replacement rubber wheels) or adjust wheels that are slipping or derailed, follow these steps: step 1. remove the laser head support the laser head assembly with both hands. use your thumbs to press upward against the two bottom rubber wheels. the bottom wheel mounts are spring-loaded to allow flex. compressing these bottom wheels creates enough clearance to slip the top rubber wheels out of the upper guide rail track, allowing you to remove the entire laser head assembly safely. note: if your wheels have derailed, you can also use this method to reseat them. step 2. replace the rubber wheels use an l-shaped socket wrench to unscrew the four bearing screws and remove the old rubber wheels. install the new rubber wheels in their place. (if your bearing screws are also stripped or damaged, replace them with the new screws provided in your replacement kit). step 3. reinstall the screws and mount the laser head securely tighten the four bearing screws back down using the l-shaped socket wrench. to reinstall the laser head onto the rail, hook the top two rubber wheels into the upper groove of the guide rail first. press downward on the bottom wheels with your thumbs, create clearance, and snap the bottom wheels securely into the low groove of the rail. step 4. check the limit switch trigger arm during removal and installation, the x-axis limit switch trigger arm on the laser head may get bent or knocked out of alignment. inspect the arm and gently bend it back to its original position, ensuring it will cleanly actuate the x-axis limit switch when the laser head homes to its zero point. step 5. perform a manual and powered motion test with the machine powered off, manually slide the laser head left and right along the entire length of the rail. verify that the movement is smooth and free of catching, resistance, noise, or wobble. power on the machine, execute a reset command, and observe whether the laser head correctly returns to its zero point and completes the reset cycle without issues. important reminder: if these steps do not resolve the issue, please submit a support ticket on zoho: https://zohodesk.1laser.com/portal/en/newticket . a technician will then be able to conduct a more in-depth diagnosis and resolve your problem.

en-242: overview laser cutting acrylic generally produces clean, polished edges with minimal post-processing. however, factors such as incorrect machine settings, poor material quality, improper focus, or inadequate maintenance can lead to defects that affect both appearance and cutting performance. this guide summarizes the most common problems encountered when laser cutting and engraving acrylic, along with their possible causes and recommended solutions. tip before adjusting laser parameters, verify that the material is acrylic (pmma). refer to acrylic selection guide to confirm the material type and recommended applications. problem 1: the acrylic does not cut through possible causes laser power is too low. cutting speed is too high. the laser is out of focus. material thickness exceeds the machine's cutting capability. the lens or mirrors are dirty. beam alignment is incorrect. recommended solutions increase laser power gradually. reduce cutting speed. verify the focus position. perform multiple cutting passes on thicker acrylic. clean the optical components. check beam alignment if cutting performance suddenly decreases. problem 2: the cut edge becomes white or frosted possible causes focus position is incorrect. air assist pressure is too high. cutting speed is unstable. optical components are contaminated. low-quality acrylic material. recommended solutions recheck the focus distance. reduce air assist pressure if appropriate. maintain a stable cutting speed. clean the lens and mirrors. test a higher-quality acrylic sheet. note slight frosting is normal for engraved areas but should not appear on properly cut polished edges. problem 3: the edge is melted or rounded possible causes laser power is too high. cutting speed is too slow. heat accumulates in the cutting zone. focus is positioned too low. recommended solutions reduce laser power. increase cutting speed. verify focus position. perform a small parameter test before continuing production. problem 4: the bottom edge is rough possible causes focus is incorrect. insufficient laser energy reaches the bottom of the material. airflow cannot effectively remove molten acrylic. material thickness exceeds the optimal range for the installed lens. recommended solutions adjust the focal position slightly below the surface when appropriate. reduce cutting speed. use a longer focal length lens for thicker materials. inspect the air assist nozzle for blockages. problem 5: excessive flashback or melt residue appears on the bottom surface possible causes molten acrylic reflects from the honeycomb table. debris has accumulated beneath the workpiece. cutting table is contaminated. material is positioned too close to the support surface. recommended solutions clean the honeycomb or blade table. elevate the acrylic slightly above the cutting surface when possible. remove accumulated debris regularly. verify adequate exhaust airflow beneath the material. problem 6: smoke residue covers the surface possible causes exhaust airflow is insufficient. protective film has been removed before cutting. smoke remains trapped around the workpiece. dirty worktable restricts airflow. recommended solutions improve exhaust performance. leave the paper protective film in place during cutting when recommended by the manufacturer. clean the worktable regularly. wipe the finished surface with an acrylic-safe cleaner after processing. problem 7: protective film melts or becomes difficult to remove possible causes plastic protective film softens during cutting. excessive heat buildup. incorrect material preparation. low-quality masking film. recommended solutions use acrylic supplied with paper masking whenever possible. remove unsuitable plastic masking before processing. optimize cutting parameters to reduce heat buildup. follow the material manufacturer's recommendations. problem 8: engraving appears shallow or uneven possible causes laser power is too low. engraving speed is too high. material surface is dirty. acrylic type is unsuitable for engraving. optics require cleaning. recommended solutions increase engraving power gradually. reduce engraving speed. clean the material surface. use cast acrylic for higher engraving contrast. inspect and clean the optical system. problem 9: cracks appear after cutting possible causes internal stress within the acrylic sheet. poor-quality material. excessive heat accumulation. mechanical stress during handling. solvent exposure after processing. recommended solutions use high-quality cast acrylic when possible. avoid excessive laser power. allow the material to cool before handling. avoid aggressive solvents that may cause stress cracking. handle thin acrylic sheets carefully after cutting. problem 10: lens becomes dirty quickly possible causes vaporized acrylic deposits on the lens. weak exhaust performance. air assist nozzle is partially blocked. cutting parameters generate excessive vapor. recommended solutions clean the lens according to the maintenance schedule. verify exhaust airflow. inspect and clean the air assist nozzle. optimize power and speed to reduce unnecessary vapor generation. dirty optics reduce laser efficiency and may eventually affect edge quality. quick troubleshooting checklist before making major parameter adjustments, verify the following: is the material confirmed as acrylic (pmma)? is the acrylic sheet clean and flat? is the laser correctly focused? are the lens and mirrors clean? is air assist operating normally? is the exhaust system functioning properly? are the selected power and speed appropriate? has a test cut been performed on this batch of material? working through this checklist often resolves common processing issues without extensive machine adjustments. summary most acrylic cutting problems are caused by a combination of machine settings, optical condition, airflow, and material quality rather than a single factor. a systematic troubleshooting process helps identify the root cause quickly wh
en-228: this guide explains why manual focusing may fail when switching from a large cylinder to a smaller one on a rotary system and provides simple solutions to restore normal f-axis movement and focusing functionality. problem description after finishing a job on a large cylinder, if the second one (a smaller item) has a diameter smaller than the rotary base rollers, you must use manual focusing to calibrate the focal length. however, during the manual focusing process, the rotary base shifts to the left (f-axis) but stops moving entirely before the small cylinder can even touch the manual focus gauge. this causes the manual focus to fail, preventing you from proceeding with the next job. source: image provided by a customer cause when you used autofocus on the large cylinder, its surface pressed the autofocus touch sensor down to its absolute limit, causing the controller's system to temporarily redefine that specific coordinate as the new zero point. at this moment, the distance between the rotary base and the laser head matches the exact radius of the large cylinder, and this physical position becomes the zero point for the f-axis coordinate system. because ruida controller motherboards run on an underlying logic that does not support negative coordinate values , the rotary base cannot travel past this newly established zero point. when you attempt to focus on a smaller object, the base hits this new boundary and locks up. when moving the f-axis to the left, it cannot go beyond the position after the last focusing. to resolve this, you must reset the coordinate system to return the zero point to its default state (the far left of the f-axis). solution method 1. execute a reset command press the reset icon in the bottom-right corner of the control panel. this will force the machine to home its axes, resetting the zero point and coordinate system back to default. method 2. reboot the vertigo power the machine off and turn it back on. it can also achieve the result that resetting the coordinate system. important reminder: if these steps do not resolve the issue, please submit a support ticket on zoho: https://zohodesk.1laser.com/portal/en/newticket . a technician will then be able to conduct a more in-depth diagnosis and resolve your problem.
en-235: overview plywood is one of the most widely used materials in laser cutting and engraving. its layered construction provides better dimensional stability and strength than solid wood, making it suitable for a wide range of applications, including architectural models, decorative signs, boxes, furniture components, crafts, and custom products. however, not all plywood performs the same under laser processing. wood species, adhesive formulation, veneer quality, and manufacturing methods all influence cutting efficiency, engraving quality, edge appearance, and machine maintenance. this guide explains how to choose plywood suitable for laser processing and highlights the material characteristics that have the greatest impact on cutting performance. understanding plywood construction plywood is an engineered wood product made by bonding multiple thin layers (veneers) of wood together with adhesive. each veneer is typically rotated 90 degrees relative to the adjacent layer, improving structural stability and reducing warping. a typical plywood sheet consists of: face veneer core veneers back veneer adhesive layers between each veneer compared with solid wood, plywood offers several advantages for laser processing: better dimensional stability reduced expansion and contraction caused by humidity higher strength-to-weight ratio more consistent sheet thickness improved resistance to cracking and splitting although the wood veneers are the visible component, the adhesive between layers often has a greater impact on laser cutting quality. factors that affect laser processing several material characteristics determine how well plywood can be cut or engraved. wood species different wood species have different densities, grain structures, and resin contents. these properties influence: cutting speed engraving contrast edge color smoke generation required laser power generally, softer woods require less energy to cut, while denser hardwoods may require slower speeds or higher laser power. veneer quality high-quality plywood uses veneers with consistent thickness and minimal defects. poor veneer quality may contain: knots cracks resin pockets uneven density these irregularities can produce inconsistent cutting depth or uneven engraving results. internal voids some low-cost plywood contains gaps or voids inside the core. when the laser encounters an internal void, it may: lose cutting efficiency produce incomplete cuts create uneven kerf widths reduce structural strength of finished parts laser-grade plywood is manufactured with minimal internal voids and is therefore recommended whenever precision is important. moisture content wood naturally absorbs moisture from the surrounding environment. excessive moisture may: increase cutting time produce additional smoke cause darker cut edges reduce engraving contrast whenever possible, store plywood in a dry indoor environment before processing. recommended plywood types birch plywood birch plywood is widely regarded as the best all-around material for laser cutting and engraving. advantages include: uniform veneer layers fine and consistent wood grain minimal internal voids smooth engraved surfaces reliable cutting performance typical applications include: decorative products precision mechanical parts model making boxes and organizers layered artwork educational projects because of its consistent quality, birch plywood is often considered the reference material when developing laser cutting parameters. poplar plywood poplar plywood is lighter and generally softer than birch. advantages include: lower cutting resistance faster cutting speeds lightweight finished products lower material cost poplar plywood is commonly used for: prototypes craft projects educational applications lightweight structures however, manufacturing quality varies significantly among suppliers. before purchasing large quantities, inspect the plywood for flatness, adhesive consistency, and internal defects. bamboo plywood bamboo plywood is manufactured from laminated bamboo strips rather than traditional wood veneers. advantages include: attractive natural appearance high dimensional stability excellent engraving contrast distinctive edge color after cutting it is frequently selected for: premium signage decorative panels consumer products gifts sustainable product designs because bamboo fibers are relatively dense, cutting speeds may need to be reduced compared with poplar plywood. plywood types to avoid not every plywood product is suitable for laser processing. the following materials often produce inconsistent or poor results. construction-grade plywood construction plywood is designed for structural applications rather than precision manufacturing. it commonly contains: thick glue lines large internal voids uneven veneer thickness surface patches mixed wood species these characteristics often lead to: incomplete cuts heavy edge charring excessive smoke variable engraving quality pressure-treated plywood pressure-treated plywood contains chemical preservatives that protect against insects and decay. these chemicals may produce hazardous fumes when exposed to laser energy and should never be processed in a laser machine. painted or coated plywood paints, laminates, and unknown surface coatings may release harmful gases or leave residues on machine optics. unless the coating is known to be laser-safe, avoid processing coated plywood. choosing the right adhesive the adhesive used between veneer layers significantly affects cutting performance. high-quality plywood typically uses adhesives that create thin, consistent glue lines and produce fewer residues during laser processing. lower-quality adhesives often require more energy to penetrate and may produce: increased smoke sticky residue darker cut edges greater lens contamination when purchasing plywood for laser applications, consider products specifically marketed for laser cutting or hobby manufacturing, as these are often manufactur
en-236: overview selecting high-quality plywood is only the first step toward achieving clean and consistent laser processing results. proper machine setup, accurate focus, optimized cutting parameters, and effective smoke removal all play critical roles in producing smooth edges, minimizing charring, and ensuring complete cuts. this guide introduces recommended practices for laser cutting and engraving plywood, helping users improve processing quality while reducing material waste and machine maintenance. how laser cutting works on plywood laser cutting is a thermal process that concentrates a high-energy laser beam onto a small focal point. the wood fibers and adhesive layers absorb the laser energy, rapidly heating until they vaporize or combust. a stream of compressed air (air assist) then removes smoke, debris, and vaporized material from the kerf. unlike solid wood, plywood contains alternating veneer layers bonded with adhesive. since the adhesive often absorbs and reacts to laser energy differently than the wood itself, cutting performance may vary even within the same sheet. for this reason, parameter optimization is often necessary when processing a new plywood material. achieving proper focus accurate focus is one of the most important factors affecting cut quality. a correctly focused laser produces: narrow kerf width smooth cut edges maximum cutting efficiency reduced heat-affected zone (haz) if the focus is too high, the beam begins to diverge before entering the material, resulting in wider kerfs and incomplete cuts. if the focus is too low, excessive energy is concentrated below the surface, increasing burning on the bottom edge while reducing cutting efficiency near the top. for most plywood cutting applications, position the focal point near the material surface or slightly below it, depending on the material thickness and lens configuration. tip always refocus after changing material thickness or replacing the focusing lens. optimizing power and speed laser power and cutting speed work together to determine processing quality. increasing power delivers more energy to the material, while reducing speed increases the amount of time the laser interacts with each point. rather than simply using maximum power, optimize both settings to achieve complete cuts with the least amount of heat. general recommendations include: use the lowest power that consistently cuts through the material. reduce cutting speed gradually before increasing power excessively. perform small test cuts whenever using a new plywood supplier or thickness. record successful parameter combinations for future reference. because every plywood manufacturer uses different wood species and adhesives, parameter testing is always recommended. using air assist effectively air assist is essential for laser cutting plywood. proper airflow provides several important benefits: removes smoke from the cutting path prevents excessive flame formation reduces edge charring improves cutting efficiency protects the focusing lens from smoke contamination insufficient airflow allows smoke to remain inside the kerf, where it absorbs laser energy and causes additional burning. for thicker plywood, stronger and more consistent airflow is generally required because deeper kerfs trap more smoke and debris. note excessively high air pressure may disturb lightweight materials during engraving. adjust airflow according to the application. choosing single-pass or multi-pass cutting the optimal cutting strategy depends on material thickness and available laser power. single-pass cutting single-pass cutting is typically recommended for thin plywood when sufficient laser power is available. advantages include: faster production smooth continuous edges higher productivity multi-pass cutting thicker plywood or lower-power laser systems often benefit from multiple cutting passes. instead of attempting to remove all material in one pass, each pass gradually deepens the kerf. benefits include: reduced edge burning less heat accumulation lower risk of flare-ups improved cutting consistency better penetration through adhesive layers if the material is nearly cut through after the first pass, additional passes generally require less energy than increasing power significantly. reducing edge charring darkened or burned edges are common when processing wood materials. to minimize charring: maintain accurate focus. use effective air assist. avoid unnecessarily slow cutting speeds. keep the lens clean. use high-quality plywood with consistent adhesive layers. remove excessive smoke using an efficient exhaust system. the objective is to minimize the amount of time heat remains concentrated around the cutting edge. improving engraving quality laser engraving plywood requires different settings than cutting. for cleaner engraving: use lower power than cutting operations. increase engraving speed when possible. use high-resolution image settings only when necessary. remove dust from the material surface before engraving. test engraving depth on scrap material before processing finished parts. wood grain and color variations may naturally produce slight differences in engraving appearance. keeping the material flat warped plywood can significantly reduce cutting quality because different areas of the material move in and out of the laser's focal plane. before processing: ensure the sheet lies flat on the worktable. secure lightweight materials if necessary. remove debris beneath the plywood. replace severely warped sheets. maintaining a consistent working distance improves both cutting accuracy and engraving consistency. maintaining clean optics smoke generated during plywood processing gradually deposits residue on optical components. dirty optics may cause: reduced laser power poor cutting performance increased edge burning larger kerf widths inconsistent engraving inspect and clean the lens and mirrors regularly according to the machine manufacturer's maintena
